newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: INTERVIEW-Waterford Wedgwood says optmistic.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Waterford Wedgwood says optmistic.

text.p: Irish crystal, fine china and ceremics group Waterford Wedgwood Plc, who reported a rise of 24 percent in 1996 profits, said on Monday that it was optimistic of another good year in 1997.
"We have set ourselves ambitious goals for the turn of the century. I am confident that we are now well on the road to deliver our vision," chairman Tony O'Reilly said in a results statement.
O'Reilly said the group's international breadth gave it confidence that it was on track to meet targets.

"In Waterford a lot of the things we have been putting in place over the last number of years have started to pay off," Waterford Crystal Chief Executive Redmond O'Donaghue told Reuters in an interview.
O'Donaghue said while January and February were not key months for sales, "All I can say is we are meeting expectations for this part of the year".
Waterford Wedgwood reported a 24 percent rise in pre-tax profits to 34.9 million Irish pounds ($54.7 million) on sales of 376.3 million in 1996.

The crystal and ceremics group, who have a 9.1 percent stake in German ceremics group Rosenthal AG, also announced on Monday that it was sub-underwriting 86.4 percent of a Rosenthal 36 million mark rights issue.
The remainder of Rosenthal's issue of 300,000 new shares at 120 marks per share, will be underwritten by Bayerische Hypotheken und Weshel Bank.
O'Donaghue said margins for the group had improved and total net margins rose to 10.4 percent from 9.7 percent while Waterford crystal margins were at 11.8 percent.
He said about 28 percent of Waterford's products were outsourced in 1996 and group profits were split almost evenly between Europe, America and Asia.

On the Waterford crystal side the group was still heavily dependent on the U.S. market with about 65 percent of its business going there, Walsh said. He added Wedgwood, which is nearly twice the size of Waterford crystal, was very heavily dependent on the Japanese market.

O'Donaghue said markets like Japan were experiencing some difficulties but the American economy was going strong. He said Ireland was extremely buoyant and it had experienced a bumper year in tourism in 1996 "... and all indications are that that will continue in 1997".
"Some other world markets are a bit patchy," O'Donaghue added. "Japan is going through a rough time, the yen has fallen and that is affecting Japanese tourists."

He said European countries like Germany and France were also a bit flat but added that the group was confident that its links with Rosenthal would reap benefits for both companies. ($ = 0.637 Irish Pounds)
